title: Single crochet join
subtitle: How to join two pieces of crochet with a row of double crochet for a visible seam
excerpt: A double crochet join (the UK equivalent of a single crochet join) holds two pieces together with a firm, decorative ridge. It is faster than sewing and becomes part of the design.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The reverse face of a crocheted piece, intended to face inward in a finished item.
The face of the fabric intended to show in the finished item.

content.text: A double crochet join (called a single crochet join in US patterns) seams two pieces by working through both edge stitches at once. The join leaves a visible, stretchy ridge on the outside. It suits granny square blankets, shoulder seams, and any project where the visible seam is part of the design.

. Hold them right sides together for a hidden seam. Align the top loops of the edge stitches on both pieces and pin or hold them flush.
Join the working yarn with a slip stitch through both edge stitches at the starting corner.
Chain 1. Insert the hook through the top loop of the first stitch on the front piece, then through the corresponding top loop on the back piece.
Draw up a loop through both layers. Yarn over and draw through both loops on the hook. One double crochet join stitch complete.
Continue into each pair of stitches along the edge. Keep the tension even; the seam should feel the same tension as the body of each piece.
Fasten off at the end of the seam. Weave in both tails on the wrong side.

With wrong sides together, the ridge sits on the outside and becomes part of the design, often in a contrasting colour on granny square blankets. With right sides together, the ridge sits on the inside and is hidden. Both methods are otherwise worked the same way.

items.symptom: The seam pulls tighter than the body of the piece
items.cause: The join stitches are worked at a tighter tension than the main fabric.
items.fix: Ease the tension or go up one hook size for the join round. The seam should flex with the fabric, not restrict it.

items.symptom: The two pieces are offset and the stitch counts do not match
items.cause: The pieces were made with different stitch counts along the joining edge.
items.fix: Pin the corners and midpoints first. On mismatched counts, work 2 stitches of the join into a single loop on the longer piece to absorb the extra stitches evenly.

content.text: Try the join in a contrasting colour on two granny squares to see the decorative ridge effect. It is the standard joining method for granny blankets and the contrast-colour ridge is often part of the intended design.
